detailed_summary: This paper experimentally characterizes two nested Walsh parity-check filters implemented on Quandela's Belenos cloud photonic processor, using a single-photon eight-mode spatial register indexed by the vertices of the cube Q3. The filters realize the classical [8,7,2] single-parity-check code (zero-sum neutral subspace N) and the [8,4,4] extended Hamming code (parity-checked subspace S ⊂ N) with one DC and three face-parity syndrome channels. The experiment focuses on leakage suppression and syndrome routing, not error correction or photon loss protection, with all probabilities conditional on postselected single-photon detections. Over 340,000 detections, neutral inputs show residual DC-port leakage of 0.02%-1.1% (mean 0.6%), corresponding to ~21× suppression relative to the ideal 0.125 DC-capture baseline and 31.6× relative to the measured non-neutral control. Injected DC contamination yields a monotonic soft error signal, and the three face-parity syndrome channels route to predicted ports with 94-99% selectivity. A sector-preserving unitary core keeps leakage far below non-neutral controls over one to three applications, with differences dominated by calibration and compilation systematics rather than gate-cycle physics. The paper quantifies these limits, including fixed-pattern separator bias, ±0.02 calibration offsets, and compilation scatter near the 10^{-3} leakage level, and reports a Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode where suppression vanished and recovered after recalibration.
key_contributions: Experimental demonstration of two nested Walsh parity-check filters on a cloud photonic processor, realizing classical [8,7,2] and [8,4,4] codes in a single-photon eight-mode spatial register.
Quantification of leakage suppression: neutral inputs achieve ~21× suppression relative to ideal DC-capture baseline and 31.6× relative to non-neutral control, with residual leakage 0.02%-1.1%.
Demonstration of syndrome routing with 94-99% selectivity for three face-parity channels, and monotonic soft error signal from injected DC contamination.
Identification of dominant systematic errors (calibration offsets, compilation scatter) limiting performance, and observation of a Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode.
methodology_analysis: The experiment uses Quandela's Belenos cloud photonic processor, which implements a single-photon eight-mode spatial register. The modes are indexed by vertices of the cube Q3, and Walsh parity-check filters are realized via linear optics and postselection. The filters correspond to the [8,7,2] single-parity-check code (neutral subspace N) and the [8,4,4] extended Hamming code (parity-checked subspace S). The setup includes one DC port and three face-parity syndrome ports. The methodology involves preparing neutral inputs (states in N) and non-neutral controls, then measuring leakage into the DC port and routing fidelity of syndrome channels. The sector-preserving unitary core is applied multiple times to test gate-cycle effects. The analysis accounts for fixed-pattern separator bias, calibration offsets (±0.02), and compilation scatter. The Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode is used to illustrate sensitivity to calibration.
results_analysis: Key results: Over 340,000 detections, neutral inputs show DC-port leakage of 0.02%-1.1% (mean 0.6%), achieving ~21× suppression relative to ideal 0.125 DC-capture baseline and 31.6× relative to measured non-neutral control (which had leakage ~19%). Injected DC contamination produces a monotonic soft error signal. The three face-parity syndrome channels route to predicted ports with 94-99% selectivity. The sector-preserving unitary core maintains leakage far below non-neutral controls over 1-3 applications, with differences dominated by systematics rather than gate-cycle physics. The paper reports fixed-pattern separator bias, ±0.02 calibration offsets, and compilation scatter near 10^{-3} leakage level. The Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode shows suppression vanished and recovered after recalibration, indicating sensitivity to photon indistinguishability.
strengths: Clear experimental demonstration of quantum parity-check filters on a cloud-accessible photonic processor, with detailed characterization of leakage and routing.
Quantitative benchmarks with specific numbers (e.g., 0.02%-1.1% leakage, 94-99% selectivity) and comparison to baselines.
Identification and quantification of systematic error sources (calibration offsets, compilation scatter) that limit performance.
Inclusion of a real-world degradation episode (Hong-Ou-Mandel) that highlights practical challenges.
limitations: The experiment is conditional on postselected single-photon detections, so it does not address photon loss or error correction.
The results are specific to the eight-mode spatial register and may not generalize to larger codes or different encodings.
The analysis of gate-cycle physics is limited to 1-3 applications, and the dominant systematics may obscure subtle gate-dependent effects.
connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and information theory by experimentally realizing quantum parity-check filters, which are foundational for quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing. The use of photonic processors and spatial-mode encoding aligns with ongoing research in quantum optics and quantum information processing. The characterization of leakage suppression and syndrome routing provides practical insights for building larger-scale photonic quantum computers. The identification of systematic errors and calibration sensitivity is relevant for improving experimental quantum systems.
overall_assessment: This paper presents a careful experimental characterization of quantum parity-check filters on a cloud photonic processor, with clear quantitative results and identification of practical limitations. While the work does not demonstrate error correction or address photon loss, it provides valuable benchmarks for leakage suppression and syndrome routing in a small-scale system. The analysis of systematic errors and the Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode add practical depth. The paper is significant for the quantum information community, particularly those working on photonic quantum computing and quantum error correction. Its novelty lies in the specific implementation and detailed error analysis, though the conceptual framework is well-established. Overall, it is a solid experimental contribution with high technical quality.
